claims.text: Subtle compositional adjustments in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its FCC subsets alter local chemical ordering.
Minor reductions in Mn or Cr reduce the stacking-fault energy.
Local chemical ordering influences stacking-fault energy.
Reduced stacking-fault energy shifts the dominant dislocation mechanism from wavy slip to planar slip.
Higher-stacking-fault-energy alloys favor wavy dislocation motion.
The shift to planar slip causes an earlier onset of strain hardening.
The shift to planar slip improves the strength-ductility balance relative to equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Modified alloys with lower stacking-fault energy will exhibit improved work-hardening rates relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Changes in dislocation behavior modulate yield strength.
Changes in dislocation behavior modulate ductility.
Identical solution annealing and cold rolling can produce comparable single-phase FCC initial states for the selected alloys.
The relationship between stacking-fault energy and dislocation behavior is well established.
Microstructural factors other than stacking-fault energy may influence the overall mechanical response.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase FCC alloys without secondary-phase formation or overwhelming microstructural changes.
The modified alloys and equiatomic quinary baseline will be processed identically and tested at room temperature.
In situ TEM, stacking-fault-energy measurements, and tensile stress-strain measurements will be used to test the proposed causal sequence.
